flags.detail: Key C is right and the question is sound, but the explanation's closing generalisation is stated too broadly: "adding a member function to a class does not make its objects any bigger". Adding the FIRST virtual member function does make objects bigger on any vtable-based implementation — which is exactly what GEN-T2U1-018 in this same batch teaches (its key C is 'declaring the destructor virtual' increases sizeof). A student reading both questions gets two contradictory rules, and the one in 009 is the false one. Verified: g++ 13.3 -std=c++17, `struct E2 { void a(); void b(); static int s; };` gives sizeof == 1, while `struct V { virtual ~V(){} };` gives sizeof == 8. The stem's own wording is also silent on whether the eight member functions are virtual; if any were, option C would be incomplete, though no distractor mentions a vptr so C remains the best available answer. Fix is one word in the explanation, and optionally one word in the stem.
flags.suggested: Explanation: change "...which is exactly why adding a member function to a class does not make its objects any bigger" to "...which is exactly why adding a NON-VIRTUAL member function to a class does not make its objects any bigger — the first virtual function is the exception, since it introduces a vtable pointer." Optionally amend the stem to "...and eight non-virtual member functions". Key stays C.

Key stays C. Stem: "In C++11 and later, an exception escapes the destructor of a class that has no bases or members with throwing destructors, and whose destructor carries no exception specification of its own. What happens?" Explanation: "Since C++11 a destructor with no explicit exception specification takes an implicit one computed from its bases and members; when none of those has a potentially-throwing destructor — the ordinary case — the destructor is noexcept, so an escaping exception crosses a noexcept boundary and std::terminate runs..."

flags.detail: Key C (operator->) is right and the enumerated list of reserved operators is correct, but the unifying rationale offered for that list is false as stated: "each one either operates on a name or a type rather than on a value, so there is no operand for a user-defined function to receive." That is untrue of at least two members of the list the explanation itself gives. `?:` takes three ordinary value operands, and `.*` takes an object expression and a pointer-to-member VALUE — neither operand is a name or a type. Verified by compiling and running (g++ 13.3, -std=c++17): `S s{7}; int S::*pm = &S::v; printf("%d\n", s.*pm);` printed 7 with the pointer-to-member held in a runtime variable, and `(a<b)?a:b` printed 1 from three value operands. The rationale is also self-defeating for the very asymmetry the explanation calls "deliberate": `a->b` has a name on its right-hand side just as `a.b` does, so "operates on a name" cannot be what separates the overloadable `->` from the non-overloadable `.`. Secondary nit in the same sentence: "the short list the language reserves" reads as exhaustive but omits `noexcept`, `sizeof...` and the named cast operators.
flags.suggested: Key stays C. Replace the rationale with a statement that does not over-generalise, e.g.: "The other three are among the operators the language reserves — `::`, `.`, `.*`, `?:`, `sizeof`, `typeid`, `alignof`, `noexcept` and the named casts. There is no single reason common to all of them: `::` and `alignof` work on a name or a type so there is no object to dispatch on, while `.` and `?:` are excluded by deliberate language design — allowing `.` to be overloaded would make it impossible to reach a proxy object's own members."

notes: All 34 questions solved independently before the key was consulted; every key matched my own answer, so there are no wrong-key flags, and I found no ambiguous or duplicate items. I compiled and ran on g++ 13.3 with -std=c++17 to verify GEN-T2U1-003 (private inheritance overrides onFull while blocking client access and the base conversion), 011/017/018 (mutable in a const member function; sizeof of empty vs polymorphic class = 1 vs 8), 012 (prints 4), 014 (prints ed), 019 (linker reports multiple definition for C::g only, not C::f), 020 (prints 12), 021 (prints 1), 022, 024, 025, 026, 030, 033 and 034 (each diagnostic matched the keyed claim exactly — notably f('a') resolves while f(7L) is 'call of overloaded f(long int) is ambiguous'), and 023 (std::move on the raw-pointer class compiles and aborts with 'free(): double free detected', confirming the moves are not declared and the copies are). All three flags come from the separate explanation-falsification pass and none of them changes a key: two are rules stated more broadly than they hold (009's 'adding a member function does not make objects bigger', which directly contradicts 018 in the same batch, and 027's unconditional 'a destructor with no explicit exception specification is implicitly noexcept', which I disproved with a compiled counterexample) and one is a false unifying rationale for a correct list (029).
